title: Bluffing Expertise at Electrode Hut
situation: A young store clerk greets Dilbert with a boastful claim that he knows far more about electronics than any customer. Dilbert calmly orders some technical-sounding parts, then asks whether he is bluffing, leaving the clerk worried and impressed.
punchline: Dilbert turns the clerk's arrogance against him by bluffing with jargon, leaving the clerk unable to tell whether the order is genuine expertise or nonsense.
summary: A cocky young salesman's brag about his technical superiority is undone when a customer rattles off obscure part names and dares him to call the bluff.

title: Dilbert Crushes the Tiny Civilization
situation: Dilbert examines a sample under a big microscope and discovers a tiny civilization. He greets its inhabitants peacefully, then tries to adjust the focus and accidentally crushes the slide with the lens. Afterward he sits with his head in his hands while Dogbert mocks him for his earlier promise.
punchline: Dilbert promises to mean no harm to the tiny civilization and then wipes it out with a clumsy focus adjustment, which Dogbert sarcastically points out.
summary: A well-meaning scientist greets a microscopic world politely and then obliterates it while trying to see it more clearly.

title: Dogbert Tempted by Catapult Button
situation: Dilbert proudly shows Dogbert his new home security system: a giant buried spring under the welcome mat that launches intruders into a neighbor's pool. He carelessly mentions the trigger button on the floor, and Dogbert, standing on the mat, considers pressing it.
punchline: Dilbert has handed Dogbert a button that would launch Dilbert himself into the pool, and Dogbert decides the amusement is worth a little guilt.
summary: A gadget-loving homeowner explains his catapult doormat to his dog, who realizes he can trigger it against the inventor himself.

title: Aging Bully Threatens Dilbert's Diskettes
situation: A bald, grown-up coworker leans over Dilbert's desk and demands his lunch money, threatening to erase his data diskettes. Dilbert calmly counters by threatening to delete the bully from the payroll computer, and the bully immediately backs down and apologizes. Dilbert then mocks him as a pathetic aging bully and offers to make him bookends.
punchline: Dilbert turns the tables on a middle-aged schoolyard-style bully with a bigger threat, then caps it off by dismissively offering to craft bookends from his old shop class, a mock-gentle insult.
summary: A grown man tries to shake down Dilbert like a playground bully, only to crumble when Dilbert threatens his paycheck.

title: Dogbert's Parallel Universe Van Gogh Theory
situation: Dogbert, resting his feet up next to Dilbert, explains the canine belief in infinite parallel universes. He illustrates it with increasingly absurd versions of how Van Gogh lost his ear, including a toenail clipping accident. Dilbert quips that in another universe Van Gogh had a dog who talked his ear off.
punchline: Dilbert jokes that a chatty dog could have talked Van Gogh's ear off, and Dogbert replies that this kind of reaction is exactly why dogs rarely share their beliefs.
summary: A dog's rambling lecture on alternate realities and a painter's missing ear gets turned back on him when his owner jokes about being talked to death.

title: Dogbert Plans Crimes, Dilbert Takes Blame
situation: Dilbert is at the kitchen counter by the refrigerator while Dogbert announces that his research shows dogs are exempt from human laws. He gleefully explains that he can commit any crime and Dilbert, as his owner, will take the legal blame. He then asks Dilbert not to be selfish about it.
punchline: Dogbert casually plans to commit crimes and frame his owner for them, and treats Dilbert's obvious objection to taking the blame as mere selfishness.
summary: A scheming dog informs his owner that he intends to break the law with impunity since the human will bear all the liability.

title: Inspiring Memo Prompts Day Off
situation: Dilbert sits in his cubicle and reads an urgent memo to all employees. The memo is full of empty management jargon about proactively improving quality on actionable items. Dilbert reacts as if he had a physical reaction, then decides he needs to go home.
punchline: The memo is so vacuous and unmotivating that Dilbert sarcastically claims it was inspiring, using his supposed racing heart as an excuse to leave work early.
summary: A buzzword-filled company memo leaves one engineer so "inspired" that he declares he needs the afternoon off.

title: Yanking a Loose Thread, Losing Head
situation: Dilbert notices a loose thread on his shirt and thinks aloud about whether to cut it or pull it. In the second panel he turns away and grabs the thread. In the final panel he yanks it and his head pops off his body.
punchline: Dilbert pulls the loose thread without cutting it, and the result is that his head comes clean off, so yanking was clearly the wrong choice.
summary: A man tugs at a stray thread on his shirt and learns the hard way that some things shouldn't be pulled.

title: Dilbert Sucked Into Computer, Meets Michael Chip
situation: Dilbert, sitting at his desk, realizes he is being pulled headfirst into his own computer program, something he has always feared. He ends up inside the digital world, where a small caped character introduces himself as Michael Chip and demands a cover charge of two bits.
punchline: The computer-world greeter is named Michael Chip and charges 'two bits' as a cover charge, a pun on the old slang for twenty-five cents and the computing unit of data.
summary: A programmer gets pulled bodily into his own software and is greeted by a pun-loving mascot who asks for a data-themed entrance fee.

title: Dilbert's Human Aerodynamics Fins
situation: Dilbert proudly shows Dogbert some odd fin-like attachments on his body and explains they are for human aerodynamics. Dogbert reacts with hesitation and silence. When Dilbert complains that Dogbert isn't sharing his excitement, Dogbert says he is wondering how Darwin would explain the fins.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically implies that the fins are so useless or absurd that evolutionary theory couldn't account for them, mocking Dilbert's invention.
summary: An enthusiastic inventor shows off strange body fins and his dog responds with a dry jab about natural selection.

title: Doctor Wants Cabaret Entertainment
situation: A doctor listens to Dilbert's chest with a stethoscope and has him cough. He then asks Dilbert to sing a show tune in the style of Liza Minnelli, and when Dilbert asks why, the doctor admits he simply wants entertainment because he forgot his portable music player.
punchline: The doctor's odd medical request has no clinical purpose; he just wants Dilbert to stand in for the Walkman he left at home.
summary: A physician makes his patient perform a musical number during a checkup to make up for forgetting his portable cassette player.

title: Doctor Dismisses Dilbert's Injured Arm
situation: Dilbert, sitting shirtless and holding his arm, is told by his doctor that he is healthy and owes fifty dollars, even though the doctor never examined the arm. When Dilbert sarcastically questions the doctor's competence, the doctor calmly points out that any complaint would come down to Dilbert's word against his own.
punchline: The doctor turns Dilbert's accusation of incompetence into a smug reminder that nobody could prove malpractice, so he faces no consequences for his negligence.
summary: A patient who got a rushed, careless checkup and a bill learns that complaining will get him nowhere.

title: Dogbert Annoys Dilbert Over Ears
situation: Dogbert, in a bad mood, decides to cheer himself up by annoying Dilbert. He walks up to Dilbert at his computer and says his ears don't match from behind. Dilbert gasps and clutches his ears in horror while Dogbert contentedly enjoys the result.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately plants a baseless insecurity in Dilbert purely to improve his own mood, and it works instantly.
summary: A grumpy Dogbert tests whether tormenting Dilbert with a made-up flaw about his ears will lift his spirits, and it does.

title: Slingshot Flight First Class Difference
situation: Dilbert buys a ticket for a slingshot flight to Elbonia's capital at the Air Elbonia counter. The Elbonian agent asks whether he wants first class or coach, and Dilbert asks what the difference is. The agent explains that first class simply means you aren't deliberately flung at something hard.
punchline: The only perk of first class is avoiding intentional injury, which implies coach passengers are deliberately flung into hard objects.
summary: An Elbonian airline clerk reveals that paying extra for a premium seat on a human-slingshot flight merely spares you from being aimed at something solid.

title: Dogbert's Opinion-Free Confirmation Hearing
situation: Dogbert sits at a witness table before a microphone during his Supreme Court confirmation hearings. A senator asks whether he holds any opinion on the right to privacy, and Dogbert claims he has never formed an important opinion in his life. When the senator accuses him of thinking they are idiots, Dogbert admits he has formed exactly one opinion.
punchline: Dogbert dodges the question by claiming to have no opinions, then gets caught out and confirms the senators are idiots, which is the one opinion he allows himself.
summary: A nominee who claims to have no opinions on anything is forced to reveal his single view of the people questioning him.

title: Naming the Self-Blaming Robot
situation: Dogbert tells a gloomy gray robot that it needs a name, but the robot insists it doesn't deserve one and blames itself for everything wrong in the world. Dogbert responds by naming it "Ruebert," a pun on its habit of rueing its creation. The robot immediately panics that people will misspell the name and that this too will be its fault.
punchline: Dogbert's name for the self-blaming robot, Ruebert, is a pun on its misery and gives the robot one more thing to blame itself for, since people will misspell it.
summary: A perpetually guilt-ridden robot is given a punny name that hands it a fresh reason to feel responsible for other people's mistakes.

title: Garbage Man's Negative Campaign Strategy
situation: Dogbert, sitting on a garbage can, tells a garbage man that voter turnout is the key to winning an election. The garbage man clarifies that the real goal is for everyone else to stay home. Dogbert then reveals a poster smearing the opposing candidate as a germ-ridden hand-washing slacker.
punchline: The candidate's real campaign strategy is voter suppression, using a fear-of-germs smear ad to discourage people from going to the polls.
summary: A scheming dog and a garbage man plot to win an election by scaring voters into staying away with a disgusting attack poster.

title: Dogbert's Poll Shows Zero Fame
situation: Ratbert reports poll results to Dogbert, who is sitting in an armchair. He explains that Dogbert's name recognition is limited to the living room, with only one vague mention from someone in the kitchen. While trying to console him, Ratbert can't remember Dogbert's name, and Dogbert has to supply it himself.
punchline: The pollster trying to encourage Dogbert about his name recognition forgets Dogbert's name, proving how obscure he really is.
summary: A tiny pollster delivers dismal fame statistics to a dog and then undercuts his own consolation by blanking on the dog's name.

title: Dogbert's Turbocharged X-Ray Waiting Room
situation: Dogbert, acting as a doctor with a stethoscope, addresses a waiting room of patients. He announces that he has aimed a turbocharged X-ray machine at the room and tells everyone to close their eyes, leave after five minutes, and wait for diagnoses by mail. He then walks off, pleased that he grouped all the hypochondriacs into one appointment hour.
punchline: Dogbert efficiently irradiates a whole room of healthy hypochondriacs at once, dismissing them with mailed diagnoses and showing total disregard for patient safety.
summary: A canine doctor blasts a room full of worrywarts with a souped-up X-ray machine and sends them home to await their results by post.

title: Diplomat Dilbert Insults Elbonian Proverb
situation: Dilbert arrives in Elbonia carrying a suitcase, having accidentally flattened the rebel leader. The Elbonians declare he must now lead their rebellion, but he insists he is a diplomat on a peace mission. When an Elbonian offers a nonsensical proverb, Dilbert bluntly calls it stupid and then excuses his poor diplomacy as first-day inexperience.
punchline: A supposed diplomat immediately insults the locals' nonsensical wisdom and then pleads that it's his first day on the job.
summary: A rookie envoy to a foreign land fails at tact within seconds of meeting the locals and asks for leniency.

title: Dilbert Sucked Into Cyberspace Pantsless
situation: Dilbert is pulled into his computer screen while Dogbert watches, leaving his pants behind. Inside a surreal 1990s vision of cyberspace he marvels at the internet and email as a network of connected minds. Back in the real world he excitedly recounts the experience at a party, mentioning that he didn't need pants.
punchline: After raving about his transcendent internet experience, Dilbert's only boast is that he didn't need pants, so the woman he's talking to concludes he's just a nerd.
summary: A man gets vacuumed into a glowing digital realm, gushes about global connectedness, then loses his audience by bragging about his missing trousers.

title: Team Lunches Without the Boss
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert, Alice and Wally that he has ordered them to have lunch together weekly to build team spirit. He then announces he will not attend because it would eat into his free time. He justifies this by saying his job is to motivate, not to handle details.
punchline: The Boss claims to be building team spirit but excuses himself from the effort, showing that his 'motivation' is just delegating the inconvenient parts to others.
summary: A manager mandates weekly staff lunches for morale but happily skips them himself to protect his own spare time.

title: Ratbert Sees Dick Clark's Hair
situation: Ratbert falls into a hole in the fabric of space while Dilbert asks what he sees. Ratbert drifts through a strange, dreamlike void, describing the secrets of time being revealed as an object approaches. The approaching object turns out to be Dick Clark's hair.
punchline: After building up a profound cosmic revelation, the mysterious object drifting through time turns out to be Dick Clark's famously unchanging hair, implying he never ages.
summary: A tiny traveler tumbles through a cosmic rift expecting enlightenment and instead meets a famously ageless television host's hairdo.

title: Dilbert's Overly Affectionate Computer Upgrade
situation: Dilbert proudly shows Dogbert a new computer component he bought, a data compression processor. He then lovingly coos at the box about plugging it in and gets so carried away that he sounds ecstatic. Dogbert, sitting in an armchair, wryly asks if the church knows about this.
punchline: Dilbert's passionate, romantic enthusiasm for computer hardware sounds so inappropriate that Dogbert jokes it might be a matter for religious disapproval.
summary: A gadget-loving engineer sweet-talks a computer part in terms so amorous that his dog wonders if clergy should be told.

title: Dogbert Judges Dilbert's Charity Giving
situation: Dilbert mentions he gave five hundred dollars to charity because of his moral duty. Dogbert berates him for not giving more while he still spends on hobbies, until Dilbert points out Dogbert's own hypocrisy and asks how much Dogbert gave. Dogbert reveals he gave a thousand and is irritable about it.
punchline: Dogbert, who lectures others about morality and giving, gave away more than Dilbert and is bitter about it, implying he is motivated by resentment rather than virtue.
summary: Two friends on a walk argue over whose charitable donation is more virtuous, and the self-righteous critic turns out to be the more resentful giver.

title: Dogbert's Evil-Be-Gone Money Scam
situation: Dogbert, wearing a yellow beehive-shaped hat, warns a man that the world will end in the year 2000 and asks for his money. He claims money is evil and that it will be safe in his special "Evil-Be-Gone" device, which is just a piggy bank. The man hands over his cash, convinced the deal is a tax deduction that earns him money.
punchline: The customer is so thoroughly fleeced by Dogbert's nonsense that he thinks handing over his savings means he is making money, since a deduction taken "from your savings" is just a loss.
summary: A scheming dog talks a gullible man into surrendering his savings to a piggy bank with the promise of apocalypse protection and a tax break.

title: Dilbert's Dinner Party Full of Dummies
situation: Dilbert, in a 'Dilbert Gets Political' strip, invites a politician to a dinner party and boasts about his gourmet cooking and fundraising for unpopular diseases, as politicians do. At the dinner, Dilbert looks around the table and asks whether the other guests are crash dummies. A guest curtly replies that it's just him.
punchline: Dilbert acts like a polished politician cultivating a pleasant image, yet at the party he notices the other guests seem like lifeless crash dummies, and is told the problem is only him.
summary: A politically minded Dilbert hosts a fancy dinner party and wonders whether his stiff, odd-looking guests are crash test dummies.

title: Sensitivity Training Goes Badly Wrong
situation: Dogbert leads a sensitivity training session and tells the attendees to close their eyes and imagine being a woman. Wally imagines that people are suddenly nice to him and hold doors open, while Dilbert fantasizes about his blouse falling off. Dogbert abruptly ends the exercise.
punchline: The men's fantasies about being a woman are shallow and self-serving (being popular, undressing), completely missing the point of sensitivity training, so Dogbert has to shut it down.
summary: A dog running a diversity workshop watches two men turn an empathy exercise into a shallow fantasy and hastily calls it off.

title: Lemonade Philosophy Needs Better Supplies
situation: Ratbert walks beside Dogbert and shares his philosophy about turning lemons into lemonade. He then qualifies it by noting that life must also supply a pitcher, ice and glasses. When a pitcher, glasses and lemons appear, he complains that there are no napkins.
punchline: Ratbert's optimistic philosophy quickly reveals itself as a demanding wish list, and even when life delivers the supplies he finds something else to complain about.
summary: A little lab rat tweaks the famous lemon proverb with a list of necessary extras, then grumbles when the spread still falls short.

title: Dogbert's Pay-Per-Opinion Phone Poll
situation: Ratbert watches Dogbert on a TV broadcast declaring that people are so stupid they should pay him to hear their opinions. Dogbert then invites anyone who disagrees to call his phone poll at two dollars per call. Ratbert, having taken the bait, picks up the phone and announces he will vote twice.
punchline: Dogbert insults his audience and then charges them to disagree, and Ratbert proves him right by eagerly paying twice to object.
summary: A television Dogbert tricks viewers into paying to dispute his claim that they are foolish, and a viewer cheerfully proves the point by phoning in twice.

title: Burning Useless Work Documents for Heat
situation: Dilbert installs a paper-burning stove at home and explains he will feed it with the pointless documents he receives at work. The Boss sees Dilbert carrying a big stack of papers home and assumes he is dedicated to his job. Dilbert replies that the papers give him a warm feeling, meaning literally from burning them.
punchline: The Boss mistakes Dilbert's stack of useless paperwork for devotion to his job, while Dilbert's 'warm feeling' comes from burning it as heating fuel.
summary: An employee turns the worthless paperwork he gets at the office into home heating fuel, while his oblivious manager reads it as work devotion.

title: Naked Telecommuting Meeting About Monkey Beards
situation: Dilbert, working from home without any clothes on, becomes fixated on why monkeys don't grow beards. He calls a meeting to discuss it, but the only attendee is Dogbert, who suggests the standard round of introductions across a table for two.
punchline: Working alone at home has stripped away both his clothes and his sense of proportion, yet he still reproduces the formal rituals of a corporate meeting, even with only one other attendee.
summary: A telecommuter who has stopped wearing clothes holds a formal meeting about an absurd question and gets exactly one attendee.

title: Converting Empty Cubicles Into Prison Cells
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that downsizing has left many empty cubicles, so he has hired Dogbert's construction company to turn them into prison cells to lease to the state. Dilbert remarks that it sounds like a big job, but Dogbert, wearing a hard hat, says it only needs paint and new carpet.
punchline: Cubicles already resemble prison cells so closely that converting them requires nothing more than cosmetic changes, implying office workers are effectively imprisoned.
summary: A manager repurposes vacant workspaces as jail cells and the contractor admits the existing cubicles are practically ready to go.

title: Open Door Policy Meets Sourballs
situation: Wally and Dilbert take the new VP up on his open door policy and barge into his office with no real purpose. They lounge on his furniture and eat his sourballs, and when he asks what they want, they casually mention that the cubicles are too hot. Afterwards they realize the candy and friendliness have made them lower their guard.
punchline: The VP's open door policy is a trap: the candy and welcoming gestures disarm employees, and Wally's comparison to a huge insincere spider hints that the openness is a manipulative show.
summary: Two employees happily drop in on a new executive's office, only to realize afterward that his hospitality was a lure.

title: Project Ends When Sun Dies
situation: Dilbert reads from a long paper printout, explaining that the project's original twelve-month timeline has grown now that the Boss has pitched in to help. He estimates the new end date as roughly when the sun burns out. The Boss responds by suggesting flashlights, and Dilbert adds that sweaters will be needed.
punchline: The Boss's 'help' has delayed the project so badly that it will finish only when the sun dies, and the Boss obliviously plans for the cold and dark rather than recognizing the insult.
summary: A meddling manager's involvement stretches a one-year project to the end of the solar system, and he cheerfully plans for the darkness.

title: Credit Card Handed to Waitress
situation: Dilbert sits at a restaurant table with a date and lectures her about never giving his credit card number over the Internet because of unscrupulous people online. While he talks, he hands his credit card to the waitress without noticing. Later, still lecturing, he finishes his point as the waitress is off with his card.
punchline: Dilbert preaches caution about credit card security online while carelessly handing his card to a stranger in a restaurant, ignoring the same risk in the real world.
summary: A man warns his dinner companion about the dangers of sharing card details online while casually surrendering his card to a waitress.

title: Intern Cuts Costs, Gets Catapulted
situation: Asok, the intern, tells the engineering team that he spent his weekend reviewing their year-long design and found a single change that would have halved the cost. Dilbert, Alice and a bald coworker listen as he proudly asks whether he can win awards for this. Alice, unimpressed and annoyed at being shown up, calls for the 'internapult' to launch him away.
punchline: Instead of being rewarded for saving money, the intern is threatened with being flung out by a catapult for making the veteran engineers look incompetent.
summary: A keen intern exposes a costly flaw in his colleagues' year of work and is met with a hostile plan to fling him away.

title: Quarterly Reviews Mean More Criticism
situation: The Boss cheerfully tells Alice he is introducing quarterly performance reviews to boost morale. Alice points out that this only means working long hours in a cubicle and receiving four times as much criticism. The Boss says he will get to hear employee concerns more often, and Alice replies that he will still fail to understand them.
punchline: Alice sarcastically implies that although the boss will hear employee concerns four times a year, he will only truly understand them once every 200 years, so the reviews are just extra criticism.
summary: A manager touts more frequent reviews as a morale booster, but his sharp-tongued employee sees them as extra scolding that won't make him any more understanding.

title: Nonsmoker Joins Smokers for Breaks
situation: Wally proudly joins two coworkers who are smoking, holding the first cigarette of his life. He announces he's eager to take the frequent smoking breaks smokers get. After he asks which end of the cigarette to light, his coworkers are so appalled by the sight of a beginner that one of them immediately quits.
punchline: Wally's cluelessness about smoking is so extreme that it makes the veteran smokers quit, while he is only in it to exploit the extra breaks.
summary: A lazy coworker takes up smoking purely to get extra breaks, and his rookie mistakes persuade the real smokers to give it up.

title: Consultant Paid Regardless Of Outcome
situation: Ratbert, working as a consultant, explains a plan to switch off the company's existing computer systems and start up a new one all at once. Dilbert asks what happens if the new system fails and the economic damage is huge. Ratbert checks his contract and cheerfully reports his pay is unaffected, and Dilbert says the same applies to him.
punchline: Neither the consultant nor the employee faces any personal consequences if the risky cutover fails, so nobody has a real incentive to worry about the company's losses.
summary: A cat consultant discovers that a catastrophic system failure wouldn't cost him a cent, and his colleague admits the same is true for him.

title: Splitting Budget Into Business Cases
situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a million dollars, but the boss can only approve up to ten thousand. The boss simply suggests splitting the request into a hundred separate business cases so each falls under his limit. Dilbert thanks him for his 'value-added' help, and the boss says it was nothing.
punchline: The boss's only contribution is advising Dilbert to circumvent the spending limit, so his 'value-added management support' really is nothing.
summary: A manager who can't approve a big expense just tells his employee to chop the request into many small ones, and gets thanked sarcastically for his useless help.

title: Patent Party Without the Engineers
situation: Dilbert asks Carol, the Boss's assistant, to schedule a celebration for engineers who earned patents. Despite the engineers being free on four dates, Carol books the one day only the Boss is available, when no engineers can attend. On the day, only the Boss and Carol are there eating the cake.
punchline: The celebration honoring the engineers is scheduled around the Boss's convenience, so the engineers are absent and the management and assistant simply enjoy the cake themselves.
summary: A party meant to honor patent-winning engineers gets booked for the one day none of them can come, leaving the boss and his assistant to eat the cake.

title: Fun Committee Chair Caught Browsing
situation: The Boss approaches Wally's cubicle and announces two items. First he appoints Wally to chair the 'Fun Committee' meant to boost employee morale. Then he reprimands Wally, citing a report showing he has used the Internet for personal reasons.
punchline: Management wants someone to promote workplace fun while simultaneously punishing the employee for having fun on the job, exposing the contradiction in its morale efforts.
summary: A manager puts an employee in charge of boosting office fun and then scolds him for personal web surfing in the same breath.

title: Dogbert Steals Dilbert's Date
situation: A woman with long black hair sits on the grass petting Dogbert and tells him she is tired of pretty boys and wants someone who will appreciate her exotic dancing and love of physics. Dilbert, an engineer, sits off to the side ignored. By the end she is happily scratching Dogbert's ear while Dilbert sobs in the background.
punchline: The woman who used to date engineers prefers a dog who will happily be petted over Dilbert, leaving the engineer heartbroken and rejected.
summary: A physics-loving dancer passes over the lovelorn engineer in favor of Dogbert, whose appeal comes down to being scratched.

title: Dogbert Relishes Sysadmin Power Abuse
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert, who is relaxing on the couch with a bag of chips, that he is returning to his old job as a network systems administrator. When Dilbert asks why, Dogbert says he likes the chance to abuse power. In the office, Dogbert dangles a new Ethernet card before a stressed-looking user, teasing him before tossing it onto a pile.
punchline: Dogbert admits he wants the sysadmin job because it lets him lord scarce hardware over desperate users, offering a taunting 'sniff' of a solution before hoarding it.
summary: A scheming dog returns to IT administration for the thrill of tormenting users who depend on him for equipment.

title: Dumbing Down For The CEO
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to rewrite a technical document in simpler terms, then keeps piling on levels of simplification for each higher layer of management up to the CEO. In the last panel Dilbert presents the ultimate dumbed-down version: a poster of a smiley face with a frown, pointing out the difference to other technologies is in the mouth area.
punchline: By the time a technical document is simplified enough for the CEO, it is reduced to a childish smiley-face drawing, implying senior executives can't grasp any real technical content.
summary: A manager demands repeated simplification of a technical report for each rung of the corporate ladder, so Dilbert ends up presenting a frowning smiley face.

title: Wally Finds Joy in Font Choice
situation: Wally delivers a technical recommendation the Boss requested, explaining that he felt powerless because the Boss dictated the conclusion in advance. To cope, he took pleasure in the only decision left to him, choosing the document's font. The Boss, oblivious to the criticism, only notes that the font explains what is wrong with it, then privately wonders why his coaching leaves employees shaken.
punchline: The Boss completely misses that Wally is complaining about being micromanaged and treats the font as the problem, while believing his own coaching is helpful even though employees leave the meeting shaken.
summary: An employee coolly describes how being told his conclusion in advance left him clinging to the one choice he controlled, and his clueless manager hears only a font complaint.

title: Double Efficiency Means Half Get Fired
situation: Catbert, the evil H.R. director, announces that the company wants to double the efficiency of every employee. Dilbert raises his hand and points out that doubling efficiency would let the company lay off half the workforce. Catbert responds by warning the group not to share this logic with the marketing department.
punchline: Catbert implicitly confirms that the layoffs are the real plan, and his only concern is that marketing staff are too bad at math to see through the scheme.
summary: An efficiency drive is exposed as a layoff plan, and the evil H.R. chief just hopes the innumerate marketing people won't catch on.

title: Dogbert Tests Obedience With Pyramid Demand
situation: Dogbert sits on the couch beside Dilbert, who is reading a Tech EE magazine, and announces an experiment to see if people like being told what to do. He then orders Dilbert to quit his job and build him a pyramid, insulting him in the process. Dilbert says he was fine with the command until Dogbert called him a dolt.
punchline: Dilbert is perfectly willing to obey a ridiculous order, and only objects to the insult, which suggests Dogbert's theory holds up and that his bluntness is the only thing that spoils the effect.
summary: A scheming dog's experiment in bossing his owner around works fine until the name-calling gets in the way.

title: Strategy Means Making You Plan
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether his project plan is finished. Dilbert replies that he needs a strategy from the Boss first, and the Boss declares that his strategy is simply to make Dilbert write the plan. The Boss then smugly thinks about how his leadership radiates from him.
punchline: The Boss's 'strategy' is just delegating his own job back to the employee, yet he congratulates himself on being a brilliant leader.
summary: A manager passes the buck on strategy to his subordinate and then basks in his own imagined brilliance.

title: Urgent Document, Coffee Stop First
situation: Carol tells a coworker she will take their urgent document to the overnight drop box with nine minutes to spare. She then reveals the box is eight minutes away and she plans to stop for coffee first. When the anxious coworker reacts with alarm, Carol casually offers to wedge the package into the delivery truck's bumper if it is leaving.
punchline: Carol's wildly casual attitude toward a time-critical delivery, including a ridiculous backup plan, shows she isn't taking the deadline seriously while her coworker panics.
summary: A relaxed assistant plans a coffee break before delivering a time-sensitive package, leaving the coworker horrified at her improvised backup plan.

title: Dinosaur's Typewriter Evolution Regret
situation: A green dinosaur sitting at a desk declares that computers aren't for everyone and that he loves his manual typewriter. He then realizes something is wrong, and in the last panel worries he needs to fix his mistake before the other dinosaurs evolve into birds.
punchline: The dinosaur's thought reveals that his typewriter-typed claim about computers contained a typo, a typo that matters only if it can be corrected before his friends evolve into birds, which undercuts his boast about a manual typewriter and implies he is stuck with the machine's limitations while evolution proceeds.
summary: A smug dinosaur praises his old-fashioned typewriter, then frets over an irreversible mistake as time runs out for his species.

title: Dilbert Finds Defects in Mom's House
situation: Dilbert feels his mother's wall and announces it is warm, then says the only way to know if that is a problem is to tear out the sheetrock. His mom, sitting with a cup of tea, begs him to stop finding defects in her house. He responds by saying he smells propane.
punchline: Dilbert, a compulsive problem-finder, ignores his mother's plea and immediately raises an even scarier defect, showing he can't stop inspecting and worrying.
summary: A son's relentless home inspection keeps turning up alarming problems no matter how much his mother asks him to quit.

title: Boss's Photography Hobby Insult
situation: The Boss stands over Dilbert's desk and announces that photography is his new hobby. He snaps a flash photo of Dilbert, who then politely offers to have a picture taken of the Boss. The Boss declines, explaining that he prefers to look at photographs later.
punchline: The Boss's reply implies he doesn't want to look at Dilbert's face in the photo now, so he prefers viewing the prints later, which is an unintentional (or oblivious) insult.
summary: A boss with a new camera snaps a flash photo of an employee, then brushes off the offer of a return portrait with a backhanded remark about viewing pictures afterward.

title: Counseling Alice By Changing DNA
situation: The Boss has been told to counsel Alice about her abusive behavior toward co-workers. He explains that his talking is supposed to change her personality, then claims any tingle she feels is her DNA changing. Alice sits silently, increasingly irritated.
punchline: The Boss's absurd, pseudo-scientific claim that a chat can rewrite her DNA shows how ineffective and clueless his counseling is, and Alice's clenched-fist silence suggests she is about to prove her reputation right.
summary: A clueless manager tries to talk a hot-tempered engineer out of her personality, promising her genes will rewrite themselves.

title: Over-Communicating Fired Over and Over
situation: The Boss tells an employee named Ed that experts advise managers to over-communicate during uncertain times. He then shouts "You're fired" repeatedly at the stunned employee. He announces he'll return in ten minutes to repeat the process.
punchline: The Boss takes the advice to over-communicate literally and applies it to the worst possible message, repeatedly firing the same employee and promising to do it again.
summary: A manager misapplies a communication tip by repeatedly announcing a termination to a bewildered subordinate and planning an encore.

title: Alice Unhinges Jaw Demanding Input
situation: Alice confronts a coworker named Lulu, who has been stalling her project, and demands her input. When Lulu doesn't respond, Alice screams at her with her jaw stretched impossibly wide. Later in the break room, Alice calmly explains her discovery to coworkers who are eating lunch, and one of them says she frightens his sandwich.
punchline: Alice's rage is so intense that her jaw literally unhinges, and a coworker's deadpan reaction is that she scares his hoagie rather than himself.
summary: A furious Alice screams at a project-stalling colleague with a dislocated jaw, then casually mentions the new talent over lunch.

title: Self-Written Evaluation Gets Honest Honesty
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to write his own performance evaluation, then instructs him to aim for a 3% raise because that is all he will be given. Dilbert then types an evaluation that says his inventions will earn a billion dollars but that he probably steals nearly as much.
punchline: Told the raise is fixed at 3% regardless, Dilbert writes a deliberately self-incriminating review, showing that the self-evaluation is a meaningless formality he can mock.
summary: A manager hands the review process to his employee while pre-announcing the pitiful raise, so the employee turns in a sarcastic write-up about his own worth and theft.

title: Fake Bills Prove Departmental Helpfulness
situation: The boss announces that the department will track the time it spends serving internal clients. An employee plans to cleverly send fake bills to other departments to show how helpful they are. Later, on the phone with someone asking for help, he refuses because he is busy with his time sheet.
punchline: The time-tracking system meant to prove the department's helpfulness consumes so much effort that it stops them from actually helping anyone.
summary: A new billing scheme meant to showcase a department's usefulness leaves its staff too busy with paperwork to assist the people they serve.

title: Delegating the Not-Caring Function
situation: The Boss tells Wally that he used to not care about his subordinates, but that has changed. In the last panel he gestures toward a woman at her desk, whose name he doesn't know, and says he now delegates the not-caring to her.
punchline: The Boss's apparent change of heart is just more indifference: he doesn't care enough even to learn his employee's name, and he hands off the job of not caring to someone else.
summary: A manager claims he has changed his attitude toward his staff, then reveals he has simply outsourced his indifference to a coworker whose name he can't remember.

title: Estate Planning Advice: Stay Dead
situation: A customer phones a discount brokerage asking for an estate plan for after his death. The headset-wearing agent at a computer replies with a flippant 'plan' of simply staying dead because nobody likes a zombie. When the customer asks about gifts, the agent answers that zombies make bad gifts.
punchline: The discount brokerage agent offers absurd, useless zombie jokes instead of real estate planning, showing that cheap service means no actual expertise.
summary: A man seeking serious estate planning from a bargain brokerage gets nonsense about the undead in place of professional guidance.

title: Monkeys Don't Wear Watches Budget Excuse
situation: The Boss holds a piece of paper and asks Alice why the software expenses in their department are higher than marketing's. Alice answers with a nonsensical analogy about monkeys and watches. An hour later the Boss, still baffled, asks whether the explanation involves fur.
punchline: Alice's absurd non-answer is a sarcastic way of refusing to explain, and the Boss is so clueless that he spends an hour trying to work out the riddle and still can't.
summary: A manager questioning a budget gap gets a cryptic animal riddle from his employee and is still puzzling over it an hour later.

title: Wally Mocks Boss's Buzzword Strategy
situation: The Boss opens a meeting by announcing that the team must do more with less. Wally responds by proposing they work smarter while broadening their focus, and when the Boss objects that this means nothing, Wally retorts that he is merely imitating leadership.
punchline: Wally shows that the Boss's own management jargon is just as meaningless as his, implying that empty buzzwords are what leadership actually consists of.
summary: A manager is told his empty slogan sounds no different from the vague jargon he uses himself when a slacker copies his style.

title: No Problems, Just Learning Experiences
situation: Wally gives his weekly status report to The Boss, with Dilbert sitting beside him. He proudly claims to have had no problems, then rattles off a list of euphemisms for problems. The Boss asks whether he did any work, and Wally says it didn't seem necessary.
punchline: Wally's euphemism-laden status report is just cover for the fact that he did no work at all, since he saw no need to.
summary: A slacking employee dresses up his idle week in positive corporate buzzwords until his manager asks the obvious question.

title: Dogbert's Tail Gives Away Stock Scam
situation: Dogbert, billed as a stock market expert, is about to go live on air. A camera operator hands him a microphone, and Dogbert asks him to keep his tail out of the shot because he'll be pushing stocks he personally owns, which makes him wag. The disillusioned camera operator thinks to himself that he should find honest work someday.
punchline: Dogbert's tail involuntarily exposes his conflict of interest, and the camera operator is so disgusted by the TV financial-advice racket that he wishes he had an honest job.
summary: A canine market pundit prepares to hype shares he secretly holds, leaving the crew member who helps him wishing for a more ethical line of work.

title: Fish Bowl Reserved for Attractive Employees
situation: Dilbert asks Carol, the administrative assistant, to book the glass-walled conference room by the main lobby. She tells him it is reserved for attractive employees so visitors aren't frightened, and when he asks for a second opinion she offers to convene a tribunal of admin assistants to judge his looks.
punchline: Carol bluntly implies Dilbert is too unattractive to use the visible conference room, and his request for a second opinion just invites a panel of admin assistants to confirm the insult.
summary: An office assistant gatekeeps a showcase meeting room by appearance, and the employee's appeal only subjects him to a panel of peers who will judge him.

title: Admin Tribunal Judges Dilbert's Attractiveness
situation: A panel of administrative assistants sits like a jury while one of them announces their verdict. They have ruled that Dilbert is not good-looking enough to be allowed to use the glass-walled conference room near the lobby. Dilbert asks to appeal and is told that appeals are not permitted.
punchline: The admin assistants hold the real power over office resources and rule on room access by looks, and the decision is final with no appeal.
summary: A jury of secretaries bans Dilbert from a visible meeting room for being too plain, and his request to challenge the ruling is dismissed.

title: Ten Seconds to Choose Layoff Euphemism
situation: The Boss gives Ted ten seconds to pick one of three corporate euphemisms: restructured, repurposed or reassigned. Ted panics and flip-flops between the options. Catbert, the evil human resources director, then asks the Boss how many people volunteered to quit without realizing it.
punchline: All three options are disguised ways of getting Ted to quit, and the Boss cheerfully admits that two out of three employees fall for the trick and 'volunteer' to leave.
summary: A manager pressures an employee to pick a fancy-sounding fate, which turns out to be a sneaky way of tricking staff into resigning.

title: Boss Invites Feedback, Explodes Over Squeak
situation: The Boss announces his new "Coffee with the Boss" program and urges Dilbert, its first participant, to speak freely and candidly. Dilbert offers a tiny complaint that his chair squeaks, and the Boss immediately loses his temper and insults him.
punchline: The Boss claims to want brutally honest feedback but cannot handle even the most trivial complaint, showing that open-door programs are only for praise.
summary: A manager begging for candid criticism over coffee flies into a rage when his employee mentions a squeaky chair.

title: Retiring Employee Fakes Listening, Fantasizes Fishing
situation: The Boss tells an older employee who is about to retire that he can now give honest feedback. The employee points out that this would take more effort than doing nothing, and instead offers to pretend to listen while daydreaming about fishing. The Boss readily accepts this arrangement.
punchline: The boss is so indifferent to real input that he happily accepts a retiring employee faking attention while mentally checked out, showing that the appearance of engagement is all he cares about.
summary: A manager asks a soon-to-retire worker for candid input, but the worker offers a lazy pretense of attention that the manager gladly accepts.

title: Consultick Warns Client, Client Ignores
situation: A horned consultant in a red jacket introduces himself as a 'consultick' (a consultant-tick) to a prospective client sitting at his desk. He openly admits he will burrow into the company, drain its money and never leave, and that his firm has a history of failures and conflicts of interest. The Boss, thinking to himself, sees no warning signs.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious or eager to hire consultants that he ignores blatantly honest warnings and thinks there are 'no red flags'.
summary: A consultant cheerfully confesses he is a parasite with a record of failure, yet the gullible client perceives nothing worrying.

title: Not Just a Cold
situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker holding a mug says he heard Dilbert had a cold. Dilbert corrects him with an absurd account of drug addiction, growing an exoskeleton, and six months of rehab and surgery. The coworker responds only by asking whether he could catch any of it from the coffeemaker Dilbert touched.
punchline: Faced with an alarming confession, the coworker cares only about whether he might catch it, showing self-centered office germ paranoia and zero sympathy.
summary: A coworker's polite sick-day small talk turns into a bizarre medical confession that he answers with nothing but concern for his own health.

title: Customer Reference Is Salesman's Own Phone
situation: Dilbert asks a vendor's salesman for customer references he can call before buying. The salesman hands over a sheet of paper, but the number on it turns out to be his own cell phone, which rings on his side of the desk. He cheerfully suggests Dilbert try again once he is in the parking lot.
punchline: The 'customer reference' is a fake: the salesman is the one who would answer the phone and pose as a satisfied customer, revealing the vendor has no real references.
summary: A vendor's list of glowing testimonials turns out to lead straight to the salesman's own mobile phone.

title: Start Building Without Requirements Anyway
situation: Dilbert tells his boss he can't begin a project because the user hasn't supplied any requirements. The boss orders him to start building something anyway so the team won't appear unhelpful. Dilbert sarcastically sums up the plan as hiding their competence, and the boss dismisses him for thinking too much.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic summary exposes the absurdity of building a product without requirements just to look busy, and the boss responds by criticizing him for applying logic.
summary: Told to build something despite having no specifications, an engineer sarcastically points out that management is asking the team to conceal its own competence.

title: Desire to Punch New Acquaintance
situation: A overly familiar coworker greets Dilbert at the coffee machine with a hearty golf question. Dilbert bluntly says he already wants to punch the man after three seconds of acquaintance. The coworker cheerfully replies that nobody ever does, and Dilbert suggests he go meet Alice, who is known for her violent temper.
punchline: Dilbert redirects the obnoxiously chummy coworker to Alice, implying she will happily supply the punch he insists nobody ever delivers.
summary: A glad-handing colleague's forced small talk earns a blunt threat, and Dilbert sends him off to meet the coworker most likely to follow through.

title: Forgiveness Over Permission, Heart Sold Online
situation: Alice furiously confronts a coworker for acting without consulting her first. He calmly replies that it is better to seek forgiveness than ask permission. In the hallway, Dilbert asks whether the man authorized her to rip out his heart and sell it online, and Alice admits he sort of did.
punchline: Alice took the 'better to ask forgiveness than permission' philosophy to a violent extreme, literally ripping out the coworker's heart and selling it, treating his vague statement as sufficient authorization.
summary: A coworker's casual excuse about acting first and apologizing later gets turned against him in the most gruesome way imaginable.

title: Topper Tops Every Rock Story
situation: At a meeting, a young coworker shows off a rock shaped like an egg, and Topper, a one-upping coworker, dismisses it by claiming a rock shaped like celebrity couple Nick Lachey and Jessica Simpson. The coworker escalates by claiming his rock hatched into an alien, and Topper again says 'That's nothing!' Dilbert watches silently.
punchline: Topper's compulsion to one-up everyone is so automatic that he dismisses even a hatched alien from a distant galaxy as 'nothing.'
summary: A chronic one-upper brushes off a coworker's increasingly outlandish rock discoveries, even when the rock turns out to hatch into an alien.

title: Naming a Company Krap2Idiots
situation: Dogbert, sitting on a nightstand, tells Dilbert (in a bathrobe) that he needs a company name so he can film an infomercial. Dilbert assumes the name should hide Dogbert's treachery, but Dogbert says that's not the goal. Later Dilbert watches TV and an announcer introduces the CEO of Krap2Idiots, which is Dogbert's actual company.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately chose a company name that openly admits it sells junk to idiots, since his customers are too foolish to notice or care.
summary: A scheming dog skips the usual deceptive branding and names his infomercial business after exactly what it sells and to whom.

title: Boss Busy With Miscellaneous Things
situation: Dilbert asks his boss to step in and make a colleague named Bottleneck Bill do his work, because Bill is holding up Dilbert's own job. The boss says he will deal with it after he finishes other things. When Dilbert asks what those things are, the boss gives a vague non-answer.
punchline: The boss's excuse for not helping is a vague catch-all category, 'miscellaneous', which shows he has no real tasks and is simply avoiding doing his job.
summary: A manager brushes off a request to deal with a bottleneck coworker by claiming to be busy with unspecified odds and ends.

title: Shard-Filled Doughnuts Are Just Delicious
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert, acting as an ethics advisor, whether it is immoral for his company to sell extremely high-calorie doughnuts filled with shards. Dogbert reassures him that nobody is being forced to eat them because they are simply made irresistibly delicious. Dilbert questions whether that is really any different, and Dogbert dismisses the objection.
punchline: Dogbert's justification, that making something irresistible isn't the same as forcing people to consume it, is a flimsy rationalization that collapses under Dilbert's simple question and is waved off with a shrug.
summary: A conscience-stricken Dilbert seeks moral approval for his company's dangerous doughnuts, but Dogbert's reasoning fails to survive a single follow-up question.

title: Dilbert Feels Disrespect Coming On
situation: Alice approaches Dilbert at his desk and says they need to talk about their problem, which she says is his utter disrespect for her. Dilbert denies disrespecting her at all. When she asks if he has even slight disrespect, he realizes he is starting to feel some right then.
punchline: Alice's confrontation about disrespect is itself so annoying that it triggers genuine disrespect in Dilbert, proving her point as the conversation unfolds.
summary: A coworker's attempt to resolve a supposed lack of respect ends up creating the very disrespect she was complaining about.

title: Elbonian Business Card Etiquette Class
situation: An Elbonian instructor in a tall dark hat teaches a culture class on how to react when an Elbonian businessman hands you his business card. His advice is to chew the card and spit it at the man's forehead. He then moves on to the next topic, dueling with yak bones, while the Boss and Dilbert sit and listen.
punchline: Elbonian business etiquette is so bizarre and hostile that exchanging business cards inevitably leads to a fight, making a lesson on yak bone dueling the logical next step.
summary: A cultural trainer explains an absurdly rude card-exchange custom, which naturally segues into weapons combat.

title: Ugly Rumor Or Ugly Dilbert
situation: Dilbert comes home with his briefcase and tells Dogbert, who is lounging on the couch, that he is the victim of an ugly rumor at work. Dogbert asks whether the rumor is ugly or whether the rumor is that Dilbert himself is ugly. Dilbert clarifies that the rumor is ugly, and Dogbert replies that he has more bad news.
punchline: Dogbert's reply implies that Dilbert really is ugly, so the ambiguity he raised was not just wordplay but a polite way of delivering an insult.
summary: A man complains about a nasty workplace rumor, and his dog's pedantic question turns into a deadpan insult about his looks.

title: Dogbert Consults Very Slowly, Billing Hourly
situation: The Boss introduces Dogbert to a meeting as a consultant billing $400 per hour and asks what process he will use to reach his recommendations. Dogbert answers with an agonizingly slow, drawn-out pause between words, "A... very... slow one." The others wait patiently while the meter runs.
punchline: Dogbert deliberately drags out his answer word by word because he bills by the hour, literally making his process a slow one.
summary: A pricey consultant stretches a simple answer across several painfully slow panels, since every second of delay earns him more money.

title: Merged CEOs Claim Married Couple Bond
situation: At a podium, one executive announces that after the merger he and another executive will share the job of CEO. He jokes that they get along like an old married couple while employees watch from the audience. He then whispers an aside, adding that the other man is the wife.
punchline: The executive's quip about being an old married couple turns into a barbed aside that casts his co-CEO as the 'wife', revealing his dominance and condescension, which hints that the shared leadership is not really equal.
summary: A merging company's co-CEOs present a united front, but one quietly undercuts his partner with a jab about marital roles.

title: Time Traveler Wally Wants Coffee
situation: During a meeting, a flash of light reveals Wally arriving from the year 2040 in a green time-travel suit. He explains that time travel is unethical only if the past is changed, then admits he came back just to get a fresh cup of coffee. He warns everyone that nothing must change because of his visit or everyone in the future will die, leaving the group stunned.
punchline: Wally uses time travel for the most trivial reason, a coffee refill, and then burdens everyone with a catastrophic warning, which makes the meeting awkward.
summary: A future version of Wally pops into a meeting to steal coffee and threatens global doom if anyone alters the timeline because of it.

title: Patty Amplifies and Distorts Schedule
situation: Dilbert asks Patty, a coworker with a megaphone strapped to her ear, to tell the project team the schedule is slipping by a week. He declines to give her the reason, saying she would amplify and distort it. Patty then announces to a coworker that the schedule is changing because Dilbert hates women.
punchline: Dilbert's refusal to explain was justified, since Patty distorts the message anyway and invents an outrageous reason that makes him look terrible.
summary: A coworker fitted with a literal amplifier proves her reputation by turning a simple delay notice into a shouted accusation.

title: Violations for Every Letter Except Z
situation: The Boss sits across a table from Wally with a tall stack of paper, explaining that he has documented Wally's disciplinary problems in his personnel file. He notes that Wally has violations covering every letter of the alphabet except Z. Wally responds by falling asleep, while Catbert sits quietly beside the Boss.
punchline: Wally, famous for doing nothing at work, supplies the missing Z by literally sleeping, and he is so unbothered by the lecture that he dozes off in the middle of it.
summary: A boss boasts of a huge disciplinary file covering nearly the whole alphabet, and the slacker employee being reprimanded provides the missing letter by nodding off.

title: Machines Have Taken Over Offices
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, points out to Dilbert that the company's network equipment enjoys better working conditions than the human staff. He claims the machines have taken over and that Dilbert exists only to power them. He ends by noting that electronic voting machines don't care what Dilbert thinks, leaving Dilbert visibly distressed and gritting his teeth.
punchline: Dogbert escalates a joke about pampered servers into a paranoid warning that machines now rule us, capping it with a jab that electronic voting machines ignore human opinion.
summary: A dog tells his coworker that computers have better offices than people and that even voting machines have no interest in what he thinks.

title: Superconductor Genius Strangled By Necktie
situation: Asok presents an invention he created on his own time, a room-temperature superconductor that could end the need for oil. The Boss ignores the breakthrough and asks why Asok hasn't completed his assigned task of finding a new toner cartridge vendor. Asok struggles to resist using his telekinetic powers on the Boss, and his own necktie begins choking him.
punchline: Asok's world-changing invention is dismissed by a boss who only cares about toner cartridges, and Asok's suppressed telekinetic rage ends up strangling himself with his own necktie.
summary: A young employee unveils a planet-changing discovery, but his manager only wants to know about office supply purchasing, pushing the employee's powers out of control.

title: Bearded Coworker Invades Dilbert's Space
situation: During a meeting, a bearded coworker leans in extremely close to Dilbert while telling a story and laughing. Dilbert silently suffers through the invasion of his personal space, thinking about the beard and the warm breath. Finally he speaks up with an oddly worded request for the man to back off.
punchline: Dilbert's request to stop 'touching my brain with your nose' is a deadpan, absurd way of saying the coworker is leaning so close that it feels like he is poking his head.
summary: A close-talking bearded colleague crowds Dilbert at a meeting until Dilbert politely asks him to stop poking his brain with his nose.

title: Boss Is Never Not Busy
situation: Dilbert tries to get a minute of the Boss's time and is told to come back when the Boss isn't busy. The Boss admits he is only free in unpredictable gaps between tasks, then tells Dilbert to have his assistant Carol call him when he's free. When Dilbert asks Carol, she also shouts that she is busy.
punchline: Busyness is so contagious that even the assistant meant to schedule the Boss's free moments is too busy to help, so Dilbert can never get any time with him.
summary: An employee is stonewalled by a manager who is perpetually occupied and an assistant who is equally unavailable.

title: Disgruntled Doug Gets a Box
situation: The Boss tells a meeting that he has given Disgruntled Doug the critical job of building the company's pricing model. He then reveals that he gave Doug's cubicle to an intern and offers a cardboard box from a laser printer as a temporary workspace. Doug, sitting in the box, thinks about deliberately underestimating costs.
punchline: By mistreating the employee responsible for the pricing model, the Boss has given him a motive to sabotage it by lowballing the costs, which would hurt the company.
summary: A manager entrusts the company's pricing to a worker, then evicts him from his cubicle into a cardboard box, inspiring a plan for quiet revenge.

title: Dogbert's Brutally Honest Career Counseling
situation: Dogbert, working as a career counselor, sits behind his desk facing a bald client. He bluntly tells the client they have no marketable talent and are permanently unemployable. He then wraps up with the standard advice to keep a positive attitude.
punchline: Dogbert delivers a devastating, hopeless assessment and then tacks on generic cheerful career advice, as if staying positive could offset being unemployable.
summary: A career counselor dog crushes his client's job prospects completely, then offers a hollow pep talk as the only remaining guidance.

title: Everything Marked Urgent Means Nothing
situation: At a meeting table, Wally tells the Boss that every e-mail he sent was flagged as highest priority. Wally explains he therefore devoted the whole week to only the first one. He then adds he'll keep ignoring an unrelated squirrel-feeding task next week.
punchline: When everything is marked top priority, nothing is prioritized, so Wally uses it as an excuse to do one task slowly and ignore the rest.
summary: A lazy employee turns his manager's habit of flagging every message as urgent into a justification for getting almost nothing done.

title: Mordac Zaps Unauthorized Computer User
situation: Mordac, the head of IT security, asks an employee seated at a computer whether he knows how the system tells authorized users from illegal ones. The computer then electrocutes the employee, leaving him a smoking skeleton. Mordac deadpans that the system doesn't distinguish at all.
punchline: The security system punishes every user with electric shocks, authorized or not, showing Mordac's indifference to legitimate users and his hostility toward anyone using computers.
summary: An IT security chief's question about access control is answered by a shocking demonstration that the system treats everyone as an intruder.

title: Lead Developer on Doomed Project
situation: The Boss makes Dilbert lead developer on a project but forbids him from reviewing the other developers' work so as not to anger them. He then admits that those developers produce very bad work. Dilbert protests that he is being set up to fail, and resigns himself to going through the motions while hoping the project is cancelled.
punchline: Dilbert's only hope of avoiding blame is that the doomed project gets cancelled, and he cheerfully encourages a bad developer to keep up the bad work, which the developer finds suspicious.
summary: A manager hands Dilbert leadership of a project staffed by terrible coders he isn't allowed to correct, so Dilbert quietly pins his hopes on the whole thing being scrapped.

title: Useless Wally's Classmates: Hammer and Nothing
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells Wally he has signed him up for a program meant to cure uselessness. Wally's classmates turn out to be a glass hammer and a bag of nothing, seated at a table with him. When Wally asks to borrow a pen, the bag of nothing points out that it has no arms.
punchline: Wally is so useless that his only classmates are inanimate objects, and even a bag of nothing is too helpless to lend him a pen.
summary: A remedial class for the hopelessly useless turns out to be populated by a fragile tool and an empty sack.

title: Elbonian Makeover Lands Finance Job
situation: Wally shows Dilbert his Elbonian makeover, a tall hat and a fake beard, claiming it hides his baldness and lack of a chin and will help his career. In a meeting he invites the Boss to take in his new look, and the Boss responds by announcing he has found his new VP of Finance.
punchline: The Boss is so easily impressed by a ridiculous costume that Wally's cosmetic disguise instantly earns him a senior executive position, mocking how promotions are based on appearance rather than ability.
summary: A tall-hatted, bearded disguise turns out to be all it takes for a lazy employee to be picked for a top finance role.

title: Dogbert CEO Boasts About Salary
situation: Dogbert, as CEO, tells a female employee standing at his desk that his salary is 400 times hers and that he intends to raise the multiple to 410 or 420. She says she hates him for it. Dogbert responds by accusing her of being selfish.
punchline: Dogbert flips the moral framing so that the employee's resentment of his enormous pay becomes proof of her own selfishness, rather than his greed.
summary: A canine chief executive brags about his outsized pay and then turns a worker's anger at it into an accusation against her.

title: Restraining Order Against Wally's Role
situation: A woman in a meeting tells Wally his role in the project is being 'transitioned', then reveals this means a restraining order, banned access to the conference room, changed contact details, and even plastic surgery to avoid him. In the last panel, a pointy-haired man asks Wally if he accomplished anything this week, and Wally fails to recognize the woman as Mary.
punchline: The polite corporate euphemism of an 'advisory role' escalates into a literal restraining order, and the colleagues' surgery works so well that Wally doesn't recognize Mary.
summary: Coworkers escalate from gently reassigning a lazy colleague to legally and surgically avoiding him entirely.

title: Lowering Dreams for the Economy
situation: Dilbert stands holding an empty mug and tells a seated coworker that he has lowered his hopes and dreams to match the bad economy. His new goals get more absurdly modest, ending with him claiming to save money by drinking only mugs of stale air. The coworker, holding a coffee mug, reacts with alarm.
punchline: The coworker is so unsettled by Dilbert's bleak, absurd austerity that he says it is scaring his coffee, a deadpan way of saying the gloom is unbearable.
summary: A downbeat employee shrinks his ambitions to fit a bad economy and unnerves a colleague with his grim frugality.

title: CEO Pirate Ransoms Himself
situation: The Boss objects that Dogbert, the CEO, has a conflict of interest because he is also a pirate who kidnaps employees. Dogbert shows that the executive compensation committee approved the arrangement in his employment agreement, and the Boss reads the contract and concedes. Dogbert then says he will phone himself to demand ransom for returning the Boss to his own office.
punchline: Dogbert is both kidnapper and ransom-payer, so the company ends up paying its own CEO to return its own employee, which satirizes self-dealing executives whose absurd perks are rubber-stamped by a compensation committee.
summary: A dog in charge of the company shows his contract lets him abduct staff, then arranges to pay himself for releasing his captive.

title: Become Patent Trolls, Skip Innovation
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that his analysis shows every future idea is already covered by overly broad patents, so the company should quit its business and become trademark infringement lawyers. The Boss objects that he has no legal training. Catbert, perched on the desk, points out that lack of skill only matters if lawyers are paid on contingency.
punchline: Catbert implies that lawyers who work on contingency get paid only when they win, so incompetence is a handicap only in that case, which cynically suggests that lawyers otherwise get paid regardless of skill.
summary: Faced with a world where broad patents block all new ideas, Dilbert proposes switching to litigation, and Catbert cynically notes that incompetent lawyers only suffer when they work for a share of the winnings.

title: Carol's Only Emotion Is Anger
situation: The Boss stands by Carol's cubicle and asks her to feel emotionally invested in the company's vision and mission. Carol deadpans that her only emotion is anger and offers him as much as he wants. When he suggests his leadership might inspire her, she replies that she feels like she's wearing concrete underpants.
punchline: Carol's deadpan insult turns the boss's attempt at inspirational leadership into something heavy, uncomfortable and weighing her down.
summary: A manager's plea for emotional buy-in is met with a secretary's simmering fury and a vividly uncomfortable metaphor for his leadership.

title: Scanner Breaks When Documents Matter
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker, Alice, to scan a document for him. She says she'll only do it if it's unimportant, because the scanner always malfunctions on important documents. When Dilbert asks if there is any room for hope, she holds up an empty candy jar and says that's where she keeps hers.
punchline: Alice's hope is literally an empty jar, showing how thoroughly office equipment's failures have crushed her optimism.
summary: A coworker explains that the office scanner only breaks when a task truly matters, then sardonically admits her hope is stored in an empty container.

title: Statue of Liberty Fish Food Excuse
situation: The Boss asks Ratbert, his PR adviser, for help because the company accidentally destroyed the Statue of Liberty and the media is angry. Ratbert suggests taking full responsibility and promising to clean up the harbor, which the Boss never did. A flashback shows the Boss at a podium telling the press the statue was old and made entirely of fish food.
punchline: The Boss sought PR advice only after already giving a ridiculous, irresponsible excuse, blaming the destruction on the statue being made of fish food rather than accepting responsibility.
summary: After blaming a national monument's demolition on edible construction materials, a clueless executive belatedly asks for crisis-communications help.

title: Business Case for Website Change
situation: A coworker asks a bald IT manager for a minor website change, but he demands a business case before queueing it. She has no time to write one for such a small change, he refuses to reprioritize without it, and she explodes in frustration. He hands her a pill, she forgets the whole encounter, and he sends her away, then reveals to Dilbert that the pills are placebos.
punchline: The manager hands out placebo 'stress pills' that make employees forget his bureaucratic obstruction, claiming they solve 20% of his problems, which means he fixes his own problems by pacifying people rather than by fixing the process.
summary: A stonewalling manager calms an angry coworker with fake pills that wipe her memory of his red tape, then admits the trick only partially works for him.

title: The Elk Had a Saddle
situation: The Boss stands at Alice's cubicle holding a coffee mug and boasts that his hunting trip was a great success because he shot an elk. Alice senses the story is incomplete, since it isn't like him to tell one without a blunder. He then admits the elk was wearing a saddle.
punchline: The Boss's elk had a saddle, which means he shot someone's riding animal, confirming Alice's suspicion that his stories always hide an embarrassing blunder.
summary: A boastful manager's tale of a triumphant hunt falls apart when he reveals the missing detail that gives away his mistake.

title: Shareholder Witnesses Year-End Budget Blowout
situation: A cheerful stockholder visits a meeting to see how his investment is doing. The Boss opens the agenda by announcing they must spend the entire leftover budget before year end to avoid a reduced budget next year, then asks how many expensive mouse pads $10,000 will buy. The stockholder grows visibly distressed and hopes he is merely imagining it.
punchline: The stockholder sits in on a meeting where management openly plans to waste money on pointless purchases, and his only comfort is the hope that it's just a panic attack rather than reality.
summary: An investor drops in to check on his money just as management plots to burn through leftover funds on overpriced office supplies.

title: Dogbert's Hostile CEO Interview Series
situation: Dogbert, holding a microphone, interviews a CEO for his interview series and asks pointed questions about why the company is profitable. Each answer the CEO gives is twisted by Dogbert into an insult, and the CEO grows increasingly nervous. In the last panel the CEO asks who will see the interview, revealing Dogbert's blackmail scheme.
punchline: Dogbert's interview series is really a blackmail racket: the footage will only stay unpublished if the embarrassed CEO pays the most.
summary: A talk-show dog grills a rattled executive with insulting follow-ups, then reveals the unflattering footage is for sale to the highest bidder.

title: No Nice Way To Insult Intern
situation: Dilbert walks up to Asok, who is seated at his computer, and warns that there is no nice way to say what he is about to say. He then bluntly hands Asok a mindless task, telling him that as an intern his time has very little value. Asok replies that a nicer phrasing surely existed, and Dilbert admits he simply didn't think of one.
punchline: Dilbert uses the excuse that no nice phrasing existed, but he admits he just didn't bother to find one, revealing his casual cruelty toward the intern.
summary: A senior engineer insults a young intern while handing him grunt work, then shrugs off the rudeness as a failure to think of better wording.

title: Ignorance Rebranded as Objectivity
situation: Wally explains to the meeting, with the Boss and Dilbert seated beside him, that he formed a kaizen improvement team to fix another department's inefficiencies. The department's own staff declined to join because they were busy being inefficient. Wally then hopes that his total lack of knowledge about their work will be mistaken for bold objectivity.
punchline: Wally is trying to spin his complete ignorance of the department as a virtue, passing off cluelessness as aggressive objectivity.
summary: A lazy employee launches an improvement team for a department he doesn't understand and hopes his cluelessness will pass for impartial insight.

title: The Pantsuit Is Talking
situation: Alice tells Dilbert she plans to buy her work clothes at a unisex suit store. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, flatly insists no such store exists. Alice complains that he always has to be right, and Dilbert replies by blaming her outfit for the attitude.
punchline: Dilbert turns Alice's complaint into a pun by saying her argumentative streak is 'the pantsuit talking', playing on 'the liquor talking' and implying her pantsuit is making her combative.
summary: A coworker's claim about where she shops for suits prompts a quibble, and the argument ends with a quip about her clothing speaking for her.

title: Wally's Anti-Motivational Meeting Wisdom
situation: Wally sits at a conference table holding his coffee mug and delivers a series of bleak, inverted motivational sayings to a coworker. The Boss arrives late to the meeting and Wally greets him with yet another twisted version of a famous quote.
punchline: Wally turns uplifting self-help clichés into cynical anti-wisdom that justifies his own lack of ambition and self-respect, ending with a twisted version of the 'what doesn't kill us makes us stronger' saying.
summary: A coffee-clutching slacker recites a string of upside-down motivational slogans that celebrate low standards and laziness.

title: Boss Suggests Changes as Questions
situation: The Boss, sitting across from Dilbert with a paper in hand, suggests changing a box on a document to say "virtual," phrasing it as a question. Dilbert takes the question literally and answers it by insulting the Boss, saying the change would make the document look like it was written by an ignorant blob in an ugly wool suit. He then advises the Boss to stop phrasing suggestions as questions.
punchline: By answering the Boss's rhetorical suggestion as a literal question, Dilbert gets to deliver an insult under the cover of a straight answer, then blames the Boss's phrasing.
summary: Taking his manager's polite-sounding suggestion at face value, an engineer answers it with a blunt insult and a lesson in how to give direction.

title: Describing Ed Behind His Back
situation: Alice tells a seated coworker to ask Ed about something, and the two trade unflattering descriptions of Ed to work out which Ed is meant. Dilbert walks up, overhears them, and asks how they would describe him behind his back.
punchline: Dilbert's question proves the coworker's insulting description of him right, since he turns a conversation about Ed into one about himself.
summary: Two coworkers casually trash a colleague's looks and habits until a eavesdropping Dilbert asks for his own review and gets an honest one.

title: Buzzword Nonsense Passes for Technical Expertise
situation: At a meeting, the Boss asks nonsensical technology questions, mixing up email with texting, clouds with Skype, and storing files on Wi-Fi. Dilbert is annoyed until a coworker explains the Boss only sometimes grasps basic technology. Dilbert then answers with a made-up reply about upgrading to a cumulonimbus cloud, and the Boss happily accepts it.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless about technology that an absurd answer naming a real type of weather cloud satisfies him as a perfectly good technical explanation.
summary: A clueless manager garbles tech terms in a meeting, and an employee shuts him up by spouting meteorological gibberish that he gladly accepts.

title: Feng Shui Consultant Replaced by Wizard
