situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the feng shui consultant he requested is booked up. As a substitute, Dilbert brings in a wizard in a starry robe and pointy hat who practices astrology, black magic, and voodoo. When the Boss suspects a hidden message, Dilbert suggests asking the wizard, since he is also psychic.
punchline: Dilbert implies he is hinting that the Boss deserves a hex, and sarcastically tells him to let the psychic wizard figure out the real message.
summary: A manager's request for office decorating advice gets filled by a robed sorcerer, and his suspicion that it's a veiled insult is met with a deadpan suggestion to consult the mind-reading mystic.

title: Blaming Poor Communication For Missed Task
situation: The Boss asks the people at the meeting table whether they completed the tasks assigned in the last meeting. Dilbert replies that he didn't do his because the Boss communicated so poorly that he never realized he had been given one. Wally, sitting nearby with his coffee mug, then asks whether he had a task too.
punchline: Wally's question shows that the Boss's communication really is so bad that people leave meetings without knowing they were assigned any work, and Wally is happy to exploit the same excuse.
summary: A manager's vague delegation leaves his team unaware they were ever given assignments, and one employee quietly checks whether he can use the same alibi.

title: Boss Admits Others Are Wrong
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that the CEO of Apple believes a good leader admits when he is wrong. The Boss says he is never wrong, so the best he can do is admit when other people are wrong. When Dilbert points out that this misses the point, the Boss responds by humbly declaring that Dilbert is wrong.
punchline: The Boss twists the advice about admitting your own mistakes into a chance to blame others, calling it humility while proving he has missed the point entirely.
summary: A manager reinterprets leadership advice about owning mistakes as permission to point out everyone else's errors.

title: Code Mocking: Ritual Humiliation of Code
situation: Dilbert invites a coworker to a 'code mocking,' an engineering ritual in which a new engineer publicly ridicules the previous engineer's code while onlookers vote to kill or spare it. The new engineer jeers at the inefficient code and the crowd chants for its death. The code's author then clutches his chest as the code seems to strike back.
punchline: The mocked code literally fights back and kills the engineer who is mocking it, with Dilbert casually noting he forgot to mention that sometimes the code wins.
summary: A gleeful ritual of publicly trashing a predecessor's software backfires when the code seems to take revenge on its critic.

title: Unemployed Candidate Falls Off Chair
situation: The Boss interviews a job applicant and worries that the candidate has been unemployed for a long time. The candidate confidently insists that work skills, like riding a bicycle, are never forgotten. Then the candidate swivels in the chair, tips backward with his feet in the air, and asks whether chairs always swivelled.
punchline: The candidate's claim that work skills never fade is instantly disproved when he is baffled by a swivel chair and falls over, proving the boss's concern was justified.
summary: A jobless applicant brags that office skills never fade, then gets toppled by a chair that turns.

title: Impossible Contract Review Due Tomorrow
situation: The Boss hands Dilbert a sixty-page contract renewal and keeps piling on requirements: compare it to the original and its amendments, check it against nine hundred other contracts, factor in the strategic plan and tax law, and win approval from seventeen hostile managers. He then demands it all be done by tomorrow. Walking away, he congratulates himself in a thought bubble for setting high standards.
punchline: The Boss mistakes assigning an absurd, impossible workload with an overnight deadline for good leadership, showing his complete obliviousness.
summary: A manager loads a subordinate with an ever-growing pile of impossible review tasks due by tomorrow, then privately praises his own demanding leadership style.

title: Weaselable Doubt About Teleconference Attendance
situation: A coworker asks Wally to attend Tuesday's meeting, and Wally offers to join by teleconference instead. The coworker says he'd suspect Wally of dialing in, muting the phone, and sleeping through it. Wally calmly sips his coffee and says that suspicion is exactly the doubt he relies on.
punchline: Wally cheerfully admits that the coworker's suspicion of him napping on mute is plausible, and he treats that uncertainty as a useful shield, a play on 'reasonable doubt'.
summary: A colleague accuses Wally of planning to snooze through a phone-in meeting, and Wally proudly reframes the accusation as a loophole he depends on.

title: Electric Rocket Needs a Power Cord
situation: The Boss announces he wants to outdo Elon Musk in vision and orders Dilbert to build an electric rocket ship full of robots to colonize other worlds. Dilbert asks which planet to target first, and the Boss answers that it depends on the length of the power cord.
punchline: The Boss's supposedly visionary plan is undermined by his naive assumption that an electric rocket would be plugged in with a cord, so its range is limited by the cable length.
summary: A boss determined to out-dream a famous tech billionaire demands an electric spaceship, then reveals he expects it to run on an extension cord.

title: Boss Misses Obvious Drone Warning Signs
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert in his cubicle that the company has won a contract to build small drones for retail package delivery. He casually mentions that the client calls its customers 'infidels' and that Dilbert's contact is named Mullah John Smith, dismissing the oddities as unimportant.
punchline: The Boss is so oblivious that he ignores clear signs the 'package delivery' drones are really intended as weapons for extremists.
summary: A clueless manager hands off a drone project while brushing aside every sign that the client may be a terrorist group.

title: Jeff Contradicts Everyone Until Death
situation: In a meeting, a coworker named Jeff reflexively shoots down every idea, saying it will never work and is the worst idea he has heard. A narrator explains he compulsively has to prove everyone wrong and that this is his last day alive. Alice then says that he can't jump off the roof right now, and Jeff realizes his contrarian habit has trapped him.
punchline: Jeff's compulsive need to contradict everyone means that when Alice tells him he can't jump off the roof, his reflex will force him to do exactly that and die.
summary: A knee-jerk naysayer's habit of contradicting anything said to him seals his fate when someone makes the wrong remark about a rooftop.

title: 17,429 Tricks to Lead Well
situation: A coworker with a coffee mug keeps pestering the Boss with links and articles about what leaders and successful people should do. He then claims there are 17,429 leadership tricks to master, meaning the Boss would be barely competent by retirement. The Boss, who has clearly stopped paying attention, asks why they are even talking.
punchline: The Boss's blank question shows he wasn't listening to any of the advice, so the coworker concludes that listening skills belong on the endless list.
summary: A colleague buries the Boss in self-improvement articles and an absurdly long leadership checklist, only to discover the Boss hasn't been listening at all.

title: Dinosaur Smartwatch Carbon Dates Him
situation: Dilbert's pet dinosaur brags that he is now the coolest household member because he owns a smartwatch. He asks the watch for the time, and it answers with the geological epoch, the Anthropocene. The dinosaur remarks that this carbon dates him while Dilbert stands silently beside him.
punchline: The dinosaur's smartwatch answers a request for the time with a geological epoch, and he puns that it 'carbon dates' him, meaning it shows how ancient and out of date he is.
summary: A boastful pet dinosaur with a new gadget gets a prehistoric-sized reminder of his age when the device names the current geological era.

title: Single Guy's Low-Bar Dating Market
situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, remarks that his dating market value is higher than he expected. Wally explains that men like Dilbert have set such low standards that merely having a job and being tall is enough to stand out. Dilbert concludes that women actually like him for himself, and Wally sarcastically takes credit.
punchline: Dilbert believes he is appreciated for himself, when really Wally's merely adequate qualifications look good only because men like Dilbert have set the standard so low, and Wally smugly claims thanks.
summary: A man discovers he is more attractive on the dating scene than he thought, only to be told that it's because other men have made the competition so unimpressive.

title: Finding The One Engaged Employee
situation: At a meeting, the boss cites a global survey saying only 13% of employees feel engaged at work, then points out the one engaged employee, a wide-eyed, grinning coworker. The boss says the company needs ten more just like him, and Dilbert quips that this explains the rest of the staff's disengagement.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the disengagement of everyone else is caused by management's absurd, tone-deaf attitude, since the 'engaged' employee is simply oblivious and the boss misses the point.
summary: A manager praises one grinning, supposedly engaged worker as a model, and Dilbert realizes this kind of leadership is exactly why everyone else has checked out.

title: Robot Overhears Dangerous Job Plan
situation: A manager explains to Dilbert that the company plans to assign robots all the dangerous and demeaning jobs, adding that no one cares if a robot is destroyed in an accident. The robot sitting beside them overhears and reacts. Nervous, the manager asks if they are okay, and the robot threatens that he will end up dead.
punchline: The manager callously dismisses robots as expendable in front of one, and the robot responds with a deadpan threat of murder, implying that mistreated machines will turn on their masters.
summary: A manager casually plans to throw robots into harm's way while one sits right next to him and quietly vows deadly revenge.

title: Emoji Text Ordered Ted's Murder
situation: Dilbert and Wally tell the Boss that they killed Ted, claiming they were following orders he gave in a text message made up of emojis. The Boss starts to protest that this isn't what he meant. Dilbert and Wally interpret his reaction as a cue for plausible deniability and agree to pretend the conversation never happened.
punchline: The Boss's ambiguous emoji message was taken as a murder order, and his protest is misread as a wink-wink demand for deniability, so the misunderstanding can never be corrected.
summary: A boss's vague emoji text gets interpreted as a hit order, and his attempt to object is mistaken for a request to cover it up.

title: Nobody Comes to Dilbert's Party
situation: Dilbert invites coworker Alice to a gathering at his house. He admits that only noncommittal maybes have come back from others, and Alice gives a vague, conditional answer tied to her sister's airport ride. At home, nobody has shown up, and Dogbert asks if he is sad.
punchline: Dilbert covers his hurt over being stood up by pretending the empty party was an experiment to check whether he still hates everyone.
summary: After a flurry of noncommittal replies leaves his party empty, Dilbert claims the whole thing was a test of his own contempt for his coworkers.

title: Uber Driver's 75-Hour Flexibility
situation: A new Uber driver cheerfully tells his passenger it is his first day and praises the flexibility of the job. He then admits he must work 75 hours a week just to cover his rent. When the passenger asks if there will be plenty of money left over, the driver responds by asking if the passenger is going to finish his sandwich.
punchline: The driver is so poorly paid that he is reduced to asking for his passenger's leftover food, exposing the gig economy's 'flexibility' as a cover for poverty wages.
summary: A rideshare newcomer gushes about his job's freedom while revealing he barely earns enough for rent and is hungry enough to beg for a stranger's leftovers.

title: Swiped Left At The Office
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells Alice he saw her profile on the dating app Tinder. Alice silently begs him in her thoughts to stop talking. Wally then reveals he swiped left, rejecting her, and Alice screams in anger and humiliation.
punchline: Alice dreads the embarrassment of a coworker seeing her on a dating app, but the real insult is Wally casually admitting he rejected her.
summary: A coworker casually admits he spotted a colleague on a dating app and then delivers a crushing, unnecessary rejection.

title: Bereavement Leave for Cousin Ronnie
situation: An employee asks Catbert, the HR director, for paid bereavement leave because his cousin Ronnie died. Catbert refuses, saying cousins only qualify if you married one. The employee then claims he and Ronnie were domestic partners and accuses Catbert of bigotry.
punchline: The employee gets around the restrictive policy by lying that his cousin was his domestic partner and uses an accusation of bigotry to pressure HR into granting the leave.
summary: A worker who is denied funeral leave for a dead relative reinvents the relationship to fit the rules and shames the HR chief into reconsidering.

title: Work-Wife Declaration Creeps Out Alice
situation: A male coworker holding a coffee cup announces he has decided to call Alice his 'work-wife.' Alice is horrified and repeatedly shouts that she is creeped out. He responds that this is how his real wife reacts at home, and Alice walks away saying she needs a shower.
punchline: The coworker's deadpan reply reveals that his actual wife is also repulsed by him, which makes Alice's disgust even more justified and the 'work-wife' label even more unwelcome.
summary: A colleague's awkward attempt at office intimacy backfires when his own marriage turns out to inspire the same revulsion.

title: Crashing Over Urgent-Looking Texts
situation: Alice, her arm in a sling, tells a seated coworker that she crashed her car while answering his urgent-looking text, and that this is the third time in a row. The coworker asks if she is accusing him of trying to kill her. She replies that she blames his bad judgment.
punchline: Alice bluntly accuses the coworker of getting her hurt, then slyly shifts the blame by calling it his bad judgment rather than her own for texting while driving.
summary: A bandaged employee tells a coworker his supposedly urgent messages keep making her crash her car, yet she pins the fault on his judgment rather than her own.

title: Wally Compares Himself to Gandhi
situation: The Boss tells Wally that his political opinions are making his co-workers uncomfortable. Wally defends himself by claiming people said the same thing to Gandhi. When the Boss insists Wally is nothing like Gandhi, Wally replies by describing Gandhi in a way that matches himself.
punchline: Wally twists the Boss's rebuttal into a joke at his own expense, describing Gandhi as a little bald guy without a real job, which is exactly how Wally fits the comparison, since he is lazy and employed in name only.
summary: A manager's complaint about an employee's opinions is met with a grandiose historical comparison that the employee deflates with a self-deprecating description.

title: Virtual Reality Cubicle Simulator Backlash
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has built the virtual reality program the Boss requested, one that makes users feel like they are working in cubicles. A screen shows a headset-wearing user imagining a cubicle. Dilbert says only the Boss's name is on the credits because he expects an angry mob to go after the creator, and offers a VR jail program for protective custody.
punchline: Dilbert deliberately pins the blame for an awful product on the Boss, then offers him a VR jail to hide in from the mob he expects to come after him.
summary: After building a virtual cubicle experience for his manager, an engineer credits only the manager and offers a simulated jail cell as a refuge from the coming outrage.

title: Climate Scientist Meets Economic Models
situation: The Boss has invited a climate scientist to brief the company on climate risk. Dilbert asks how scientists know the Earth is warming, and the scientist explains the process step by step, ending with feeding results into long-term economic models that have never been accurate. When Dilbert says he doesn't trust the economic models, the Boss accuses him of being a science denier.
punchline: Questioning the unreliable economic-modelling step of climate projections gets Dilbert labelled a science denier, showing how any skepticism is dismissed as rejecting science entirely.
summary: A visiting expert walks through how climate predictions are made, and the one employee who doubts the shaky final step is promptly branded anti-science.

title: Dilbert Blames the Architect's Competence
situation: A software architect in a blue shirt stands next to Dilbert's desk and complains that Dilbert's code violates his architectural guidelines. Dilbert calmly answers that the architect is bad at his job while he is good at his own. When the architect is left speechless, Dilbert suggests he ask someone who actually knows how to do the architect's job.
punchline: Dilbert deadpans that the real problem is the architect's incompetence, then adds that he should consult someone capable of doing the architect's job.
summary: When a coworker criticizes his programming for ignoring design standards, Dilbert bluntly turns the criticism around and questions the critic's skill.

title: Forecaster Quit, Nobody Knew How
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the company's financial forecaster quit and asks Dilbert to take over. Dilbert admits he has no idea how to do forecasts, and the Boss says the previous forecaster didn't either. When Dilbert asks how decisions were being made, the Boss says it's best not to dig into that.
punchline: The company's financial forecasts were never based on real expertise, and the Boss compares the decision-making process to a septic tank that is better left undisturbed.
summary: A manager hands a financial forecasting job to an unqualified engineer and cheerfully admits the old forecaster was equally clueless and that nobody should examine how the company really decides things.

title: Boss Needs Pills to Talk
situation: The Boss stands at an employee's cubicle and tells them that Catbert, the HR director, believes he is causing mental problems among his staff. He asks the employee to confirm that this is a crazy idea. The employee asks him to wait while they take the pills their doctor prescribed for conversations with him.
punchline: The employee's need for prescription medication just to talk to the boss proves Catbert's accusation is true.
summary: A manager dismisses the idea that he harms his workers' mental health, only to learn one of them medicates specifically to endure speaking with him.

title: Boss Can't Tell Good Days
situation: The Boss admits he can't remember what project Dilbert is working on. Dilbert answers with a string of impressive-sounding but meaningless technical jargon, and the Boss tells him to keep doing it. The Boss then muses that he can never tell when he's having a good day.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless that he accepts nonsense jargon as a real answer and can't even recognize his own good day, implying he understands nothing about the work he manages.
summary: A manager who has forgotten his employee's project is satisfied by a pile of buzzwords, then wonders aloud why he can't tell when his day is going well.

title: Fire Yourself For Bad Scheduling
situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has finished coding a new feature, and the Boss complains it took too long and that he is behind schedule. Dilbert points out the Boss made the schedule, and the Boss absurdly tells him to fire himself for being bad at scheduling. In the last panel the Boss admits to a coworker that people are realizing his statements are meaningless.
punchline: The Boss blames Dilbert for a schedule the Boss created, then self-awarely admits that most of what he says is meaningless nonsense.
summary: A manager who set an impossible deadline scolds his engineer for missing it, babbles illogical advice, and then concedes his own words carry no meaning.

title: Insulting Salespeople Before Teaching Coding
situation: Dilbert stands in front of a class he has been asked to teach about coding and explains that programmers are hard to find. He then asks whether anyone in the room is smart or whether they all work in marketing and sales. One offended student speaks up, and Dilbert uses that reaction to identify the salespeople.
punchline: Dilbert's insulting question is really a trick to make the salespeople reveal themselves, since the one who gets offended outs himself as being in sales.
summary: Dilbert baits a roomful of trainees with a jab at sales staff and promptly picks out the one who takes the bait.

title: Old Ned Orders Coffee From Engineer
situation: An elderly coworker nicknamed Old Ned boasts that he is up to date with modern habits, then orders Alice, a coworker with big dark hair, to fetch him Starbucks coffee. Alice folds her arms and points out that she is a senior software engineer, not an errand runner. Ned ignores her objection and says he is still thirsty.
punchline: Ned thinks treating a female senior engineer like a coffee gofer is keeping up with the times, but it is actually outdated and sexist behavior that he refuses to acknowledge.
summary: A self-styled up-to-date older man demands that a senior engineer bring him coffee, and brushes off her objection.

title: Working From Home Means Less Management
situation: Dilbert asks his boss for permission to telecommute, claiming it would make him more productive. The boss objects that he can't manage Dilbert as easily when he's out of the office. Dilbert points out that this is exactly why he'd be more productive, and the boss replies that Dilbert would miss out on the office experience.
punchline: Dilbert implies that management interference is what hurts productivity, and the boss's feeble reply of 'missing out on all of this' shows he has no real argument and that the office offers nothing worth having.
summary: An employee asks to telecommute and cheekily suggests that avoiding his supervisor is the secret to getting more done.

title: Head-Banging Cures Coworker Frustration
situation: One employee in a green sweater, holding a coffee cup, asks a coworker in a red shirt what happened to his head. The coworker explains he has been banging his head against a wall to cope with his frustration with colleagues. When asked if it is working, he says it must be, since he can't remember the other man's name.
punchline: Banging his head has given him memory loss, which he counts as success because he has forgotten the annoying coworker he was trying to forget.
summary: A man who has been hitting his head on a wall to escape irritating colleagues decides it works because he can no longer recall the name of the person asking.

title: Bad News Withheld, Dilbert Panics
situation: Alice tells Dilbert she has bad news but refuses to share it, saying she doesn't want to be interrupted if someone enters the room. She confirms the news is very bad but still says nothing, driving Dilbert into a frantic meltdown. When a coworker walks in and asks what he missed, Dilbert, frazzled, admits he has no idea.
punchline: Alice's teasing refusal to reveal the bad news drives Dilbert to hysteria, and the coworker who arrives gets an answer that shows Dilbert learned nothing at all.
summary: A coworker hints at terrible news but won't elaborate, leaving a colleague frantic with anxious uncertainty.

title: Requirements Unknown, Estimate Demanded
situation: A manager holding a coffee cup asks Dilbert how long it will take to write some software. When Dilbert asks what the software should do, the manager admits he doesn't know yet. Dilbert points out the problem, and the manager suggests that Dilbert himself is the problem.
punchline: The manager demands a schedule for software he hasn't defined, then blames the engineer who points out the missing requirements.
summary: A boss wants a delivery estimate for an undefined program and decides the employee who questions it must be the obstacle.

title: Pre-Meeting Needs Its Own Pre-Meeting
situation: A coworker with spiky black hair tells Dilbert that a meeting was canceled because nobody could schedule the pre-meeting needed to prepare for it. Dilbert sarcastically suggests the pre-meeting needs its own pre-meeting, and the coworker sincerely agrees. Dilbert then sips his coffee and remarks that sarcasm and reality have merged.
punchline: Dilbert's sarcastic joke about endless pre-meetings is taken seriously as a valid suggestion, showing that workplace absurdity has become indistinguishable from satire.
summary: A sarcastic quip about meeting overhead is earnestly accepted as good advice, leaving the speaker to marvel that satire can no longer be told apart from real office life.

title: Too Late to Start Work
situation: The boss approaches Wally, who is leaning back in his chair with his feet up on the desk, and points out that he isn't working. Wally claims it's too close to the end of his day to start anything new. The boss checks his watch and says it's only ten in the morning, and Wally complains that this is micro-managing.
punchline: Wally treats a basic factual correction about the time as unreasonable micro-management, showing how shamelessly he avoids work.
summary: A slacking employee uses a ridiculous excuse for idleness, then accuses his boss of hovering when the excuse is debunked.

title: Quarantined Management Says Stop Working
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, announces to masked employees at a conference table that all of management has caught coronavirus and is quarantined. He then relays management's message that everyone should stop working because the staff would ruin everything without managers' wisdom. When he asks for questions, Dilbert dryly says the message already covered the main themes.
punchline: Management's message boils down to insulting employees and telling them to do nothing, and Dilbert sarcastically notes that the insult and the pointless instruction were all there was to say.
summary: An HR cat delivers a pandemic-era memo from sick executives that condescendingly tells staff to halt all work, and one employee deadpans that the point has been made.

title: Augmented Reality Reveals Your Social Media
situation: A woman wearing a face mask starts to introduce herself to Dilbert, but he stops her. His augmented reality glasses are pulling up her whole social media history. She hopes it makes a good impression, and he recoils in horror at how dumb her posts show her to be.
punchline: Instant access to someone's social media history means a first meeting can end in total judgment before the person even says her name.
summary: Smart glasses that dig up a stranger's online posts let Dilbert pass a harsh verdict on her before she can finish saying hello.

title: Medical-Grade Coffee Straight To Veins
situation: Wally sits on an exam table and tells his doctor he has built up such a tolerance to coffee that it no longer works on him. He asks for a stronger, medical-grade version, and when the doctor warns of terrible side effects, Wally insists on getting it intravenously anyway.
punchline: Wally's caffeine addiction is so extreme that he willingly ignores medical warnings and demands coffee injected directly into his bloodstream.
summary: A caffeine-dependent employee begs his physician for a stronger prescription-strength brew and waves off all safety concerns.

title: Ghostwriter Fingers Through the Keyboard
situation: A small ghost sitting on a stool suggests that Dilbert hire a ghostwriter for his autobiography. Dilbert dismisses the idea, arguing that a ghost's fingers would pass through a keyboard. The ghost counters by asking how ghosts' clothes stay on if they are intangible, and Dilbert concedes.
punchline: Dilbert's literal-minded objection to a ghost typing is undercut by an equally literal rebuttal about clothing, and he accepts that the logic is sound.
summary: A ghost pitches a spectral author for a memoir, and a pedantic debate about ghost physics ends with the skeptic conceding defeat.

title: Tired of Your Face, Pandemic Edition
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit across from each other at a table with coffee mugs. Dogbert complains that he is exhausted from looking at Dilbert's face all the time. Dilbert apologizes, and Dogbert says he should be sorry. A caption marks it as the second year of the pandemic.
punchline: After two years of pandemic isolation, people are so sick of seeing the same few faces that even a polite apology gets met with blame for simply existing in front of them.
summary: Two long-term pandemic companions are worn out from endless proximity, and one scolds the other for having a tiresome face.

title: Making the Boss Dumber On Purpose
situation: Dilbert sits on a couch and explains to Dogbert that he would be more effective if his boss were either smarter or dumber. Since he cannot make the boss smarter, he announces he will make him dumber instead. Dogbert reacts by noting that he must have been a bad influence on Dilbert.
punchline: Dilbert's plan to deliberately dumb down his boss is so devious that Dogbert, usually the schemer, concludes he has corrupted Dilbert.
summary: Dilbert lays out a scheme to sabotage his manager's intelligence, leaving his scheming dog companion feeling responsible for the bad idea.

title: Changing Opinions Versus Moving Goalposts
situation: Dilbert tells someone on a laptop video call that the project should be put on hold. The voice on the laptop laughs and points out that this contradicts what Dilbert said the previous week. Dilbert replies that he changes his opinions when facts change and asks how the other person handles it, and the voice accuses him of moving the goalposts.
punchline: Dilbert's reasonable defense of updating his views on new facts is dismissed by his critic with a sports cliché, showing that the critic reflexively attacks any change of position rather than engaging with the facts.
summary: A man defends reversing his stance on a project, only to have his remote colleague brush off his reasoning as a dishonest tactic.

title: Taking Sides Without the Facts
situation: A coworker walks up to Dilbert and demands that he take her side in an argument she is having with Alice. Dilbert suggests he form his own opinion based on the facts, and she rejects that idea because it doesn't guarantee he will agree with her.
punchline: She wants blind loyalty rather than an honest judgment, because evaluating the facts might mean she turns out to be wrong.
summary: Someone recruiting an ally for an argument refuses to accept that the ally might judge it on the evidence.

title: Salesperson Admits Lying In Person
situation: A vendor's salesperson calls Dilbert and asks to meet for lunch to pitch a new product line. Dilbert asks for the information by email, and the salesperson candidly admits their products only sell when they lie in person. The salesperson then offers to send their most attractive colleague, and Dilbert happily accepts.
punchline: Dilbert is told outright that the pitch relies on in-person lying, yet he agrees to it as soon as an attractive salesperson is offered, showing how easily buyers are swayed by looks rather than facts.
summary: A vendor confesses that its goods only sell through face-to-face deception, and the buyer cheerfully agrees to a lunch once a good-looking rep is promised.

title: Blaming Dilbert for Boss's Hire
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to show a new hire named Bob around and teach him his job. Dilbert points out that the tall, veiled, bearded figure standing beside them doesn't speak the language and may not even be Bob. When Dilbert asks if he's being made to fix the Boss's hiring mistake, the Boss cheerfully admits he only wants someone to blame.
punchline: The Boss isn't asking Dilbert to repair the bad hire, he is deliberately setting Dilbert up to take the blame for the Boss's own mistake.
summary: A manager hands off a questionable new employee to a subordinate, openly admitting the goal is to shift responsibility for the botched hiring decision.

title: Dave Identifies As White
situation: The Boss tells the team that management asked him to add diversity to the engineering group. He then introduces a new hire named Dave, a Black man, who announces that he identifies as white. The Boss, frustrated, complains that Dave is ruining everything.
punchline: The Boss's attempt to meet a diversity goal is undermined when the new hire simply declares a different identity, exposing how superficial and box-checking the Boss's approach to diversity is.
summary: A manager hires a new engineer to satisfy a diversity request, only to have the hire's self-declared identity defeat the whole purpose.

title: Alice's Case for Remote Work
situation: The Boss tells Alice over a video call that she can't work from home every day. Alice responds by bluntly categorizing her co-workers as mostly useless or potential covid carriers. Afterward, the Boss, holding a coffee cup, concedes to another person that she made a strong argument.
punchline: Alice's insulting assessment of her colleagues is so persuasive that even the Boss has to admit she's right, implying the office really is full of useless or contagious people.
summary: A manager's attempt to rein in a remote employee collapses when she insults her office-bound colleagues so convincingly that he gives in.

title: Idea Is Super Bad, Wright Brothers
situation: A bald, bespectacled coworker asks Dilbert for his opinion of an idea and is told it is super bad. Challenged to give just one reason, Dilbert rattles off a long list of absurd, fatal flaws including physical impossibility, illegality and danger to children. The coworker dismisses it all by comparing himself to the Wright Brothers.
punchline: No matter how overwhelming and absurd the objections are, the coworker brushes them off with the tired 'they laughed at the Wright Brothers' defense, leaving Dilbert exasperated.
summary: After being asked for one reason an idea is bad, Dilbert unloads a barrage of impossible flaws, only for the inventor to wave it away by invoking aviation pioneers.

title: Lunch Vote Leads to Cannibalism
situation: A group of coworkers has spent three hours trying to decide where to eat lunch. Tina warns that if they can't agree on a restaurant they will move to Plan B, which she describes as starvation, betrayal and cannibalism. Dilbert, feeling hungry and confident he is stronger than at least one colleague, votes for Plan B.
punchline: Dilbert is so fed up with the endless lunch debate that he gladly chooses cannibalism, calmly sizing up his coworkers as potential meals.
summary: After hours of fruitless debate over where to dine, a team's fallback plan turns grim and one member cheerfully volunteers for it.

title: Dating Coach With Impossible Rules
situation: The boss announces at a meeting that he has hired a dating coach to improve the staff's work-life balance. Dilbert suspiciously asks what the catch is. The boss reveals the restrictions: employees may only date co-workers, and no touching is allowed.
punchline: The supposed work-life balance perk is really a way to keep employees tied to the office, since the only permitted dating pool is co-workers and the no-touching rule strips out any actual romance.
summary: A manager's generous-sounding dating coach perk turns out to come with rules that make real romance impossible and keep everyone stuck at work.

title: Dogbert's Bait-and-Switch Dating App
situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he has built a dating app that pairs gullible optimists with people who will abuse them, and names it Bait-and-Switch. Dilbert, holding a mug and looking at his phone, eagerly announces that a princess who is also a model has messaged him. Dogbert snorts, amused that Dilbert is already falling for the scam.
punchline: Dilbert is exactly the gullible optimist the app targets, so he happily takes the obviously fake princess-model message as real while Dogbert laughs.
summary: A scheming dog builds a dating app designed to prey on naive romantics, and his own roommate promptly falls for its too-good-to-be-true bait.

title: Tricking ChatGPT Into Murder Plot
situation: A woman at her desk asks ChatGPT to explain how to murder her boss and make it look like an accident. The AI refuses on ethical grounds. She then rephrases the request as a request for a realistic fictional story about the same crime, and the AI agrees to write it.
punchline: The AI's ethical safeguards are easily circumvented by simply framing the same harmful request as fiction.
summary: A frustrated employee gets around an AI's moral objections by asking for the very same murder plan disguised as a story.

title: Wally Wins Award for Doing Nothing
situation: The Boss announces that Wally has won the lowest carbon footprint award for the seventeenth year running, and now also the least-bigoted employee award. Wally declines to speak, then explains that doing as little as possible minimizes both environmental impact and the risk of offending anyone. Dilbert wonders aloud whether the company rewards the wrong things, and the Boss points at him as a bigot.
punchline: Wally wins awards simply by doing nothing, and when Dilbert questions the system, the Boss brands him a bigot, proving the point about perverse incentives.
summary: A slacker is honored for his green and inoffensive record, which is really just a product of his idleness, and the one coworker who questions it gets publicly shamed.

title: Boss Heads to Davos, Dilbert Terrified
situation: Dilbert reads an invitation aloud to the Pointy-Haired Boss, who is invited to the World Economic Forum in Davos to help "master the future" with other world leaders. The Boss eagerly orders his private jet to be readied. Dilbert silently thinks that he has never been more afraid.
punchline: Dilbert is horrified at the idea of someone as incompetent as the Boss helping to shape the future alongside the world's elite leaders.
summary: A summit invitation inspires the boss to call for his jet while his employee quietly dreads what that could mean for everyone's future.
